title: AquaWatch Water Risk Ranking
subtitle: Ranking water risk for every municipality in Ceará, Brazil, and showing how far to trust each score
problem: Field teams needed to know which of Ceará's 184 municipalities faced the highest water risk, but 142 of them (77%) had no utility records. A simple ranking would have hidden how uncertain it really was.
approach: I joined census, utility and satellite data in one reproducible pipeline, normalized risk by percentile rank instead of min-max scaling so outliers like Fortaleza and Jaguaribara could not distort the index, and let K-means find natural tier breakpoints instead of imposing policy thresholds.
built: A 13-step Python pipeline over IBGE Census, SNIS utility and JRC satellite data, zonal statistics on 338MB of raster tiles with Rasterio and GeoPandas, a 0.05 to 0.774 risk index, K-means tiers, a 3-dimension confidence framework, worst-case sensitivity analysis, and a verify_priority field for a dispatch-ready verification table.
value: All 184 municipalities ranked into 55 Critical, 65 High, 40 Medium and 24 Low tiers, with a verification table that tells field teams where to check first.

twists.title: The missing data was the finding
twists.text: 77% of municipalities had no utility records. Instead of quietly filling the gap, I built a confidence framework, and it flagged none of the 55 Critical ratings as high-confidence.

twists.title: Min-max scaling would have misled
twists.text: A few extreme municipalities would have squeezed everyone else together, so I normalized every risk variable by percentile rank.

twists.title: Tiers came from the data, not a policy line
twists.text: K-means (k=4) found natural breakpoints, and a worst-case sensitivity test (0% coverage imputation) checked how stable each tier was before anything reached the field.

title: Nexodus Data Automation
subtitle: Turning disconnected KPIs into a repeatable reporting system
problem: Zoho Social and Zoho CRM held different pieces of the business picture. Reporting required repeated extraction, reconciliation, and manual checks, so numbers were slow and inconsistent.
approach: I mapped the KPI sources first, audited existing records for mismatches, and designed the workflow around the real business-review cycle.
built: Python and Selenium extraction, five Power BI dashboards, DAX measures, refresh workflows, historical retention, and audits across 1,000+ records.
value: The team moved to one reporting flow and reduced recurring KPI reporting time by 70%.

twists.title: The dashboard was not step one
twists.text: I first had to understand why numbers disagreed across systems. Validation and reconciliation came before visualization.

twists.title: History was part of the solution
twists.text: The workflow also needed to preserve data beyond the source platform's retention limits.

twists.title: The real win was time
twists.text: The strongest outcome was not technical complexity. It was giving the team back hours every reporting cycle.

title: Nexodus NLP & Data Quality
subtitle: Building trust in structured data before analyzing unstructured content
problem: Daily CRM and social data had no validation layer, while audience perception was hidden inside more than 1,000 captions and comments.
approach: I separated the work into structured-data validation for reporting trust and BERT-based NLP for recurring audience patterns.
built: MySQL and Pandas validation workflows, preprocessing, tokenization, BERT analysis, and stakeholder-ready reporting notes.
value: 15+ issues were caught weekly before downstream reporting, and content discussions moved from intuition toward evidence.

twists.title: AI was not the first problem
twists.text: Basic field and formatting errors could damage reporting before any model was used.

twists.title: Themes needed translation
twists.text: Topic and sentiment outputs mattered only after they were explained in business language.

twists.title: Trust came before sophistication
twists.text: Clean inputs and documented assumptions created more value than model tuning alone.

title: AnaChart Analyst Accuracy
subtitle: Making analyst recommendations comparable and measurable
problem: 55,106 recommendations across 98 NASDAQ-100 stocks used 164 rating labels, making comparison unreliable. The baseline model was barely better than random.
approach: I standardized the labels, used leakage-aware validation, and engineered stock-difficulty and analyst-momentum features.
built: BigQuery analytical tables, systematic label mapping, XGBoost models, analyst segmentation, and a Streamlit prototype.
value: AUC improved from 0.59 to 0.857, creating a clearer way to compare analyst performance and understand accuracy drivers.

twists.title: Cleaning created the comparison layer
twists.text: Reducing 164 labels into five consistent segments was the foundation of the model.

twists.title: Accuracy needed context
twists.text: Analyst performance changes when the stock itself is difficult to predict.

twists.title: Recent behavior carried signal
twists.text: Momentum features added information that long-run averages missed.

title: Traxidy Risk Analytics
subtitle: Turning fragmented project records into cross-project risk signals
problem: Project performance data lived in 76 SQL tables, and teams defined delay and status differently. Leadership lacked a consistent cross-project view.
approach: I reduced the data model, standardized GYR and delay definitions, and focused the analysis on actionable root causes.
built: Eleven analytical tables, operational KPIs, Random Forest and LSTM models, Tableau dashboards, and a chatbot prototype.
value: The analysis surfaced resource constraints and scope changes as major delay drivers, helping leadership prioritize interventions.

twists.title: More tables did not create more insight
twists.text: The key move was reducing 76 scattered tables into 11 usable structures.

twists.title: Definitions had to be fixed first
twists.text: A model cannot learn consistently when teams label risk differently.

twists.title: The chatbot was an access layer
twists.text: Its value came from making trusted metrics easier to reach, not from being the main product.

title: Warehouse Sales Intelligence
subtitle: A full decision system built around validation before modeling
problem: 307,000+ records contained a $7,800 anomaly, an 83% gap in 2018, leakage risks, uncertain seasonality, and insights locked inside technical tools.
approach: I built the project in layers: audit, Medallion architecture, leakage-safe modeling, statistical testing, forecasting, then conversational access.
built: Bronze-Silver-Gold pipeline, DuckDB, XGBoost, Prophet, A/B testing, drift detection, and an AI agent with human approval.
value: 77% honest demand accuracy, a $271,070 seasonal opportunity, and a $462,768 November peak forecast.

twists.title: The first accuracy was too good
twists.text: Three leakage types inflated performance. Fixing them lowered the number but made it honest.

twists.title: The summer spike needed proof
twists.text: Statistical testing showed Beer drove 95% of the seasonal premium while Wine and Kegs behaved differently.

twists.title: The AI layer came last
twists.text: The agent became useful only after SQL, model, and forecast outputs were stable and reviewable.

title: Hospital Readmission Risk
subtitle: Turning fragmented EHR history into an actionable early-warning signal
problem: Patient data was spread across 16 relational tables with duplicate IDs, overlapping dates, and inconsistent care episodes.
approach: I resolved identity and time alignment first, engineered clinically meaningful features, and used leakage-safe evaluation.
built: PostgreSQL integration, keyed joins, date alignment, clinically informed imputation, 22 features, stratified validation, and Streamlit.
value: The model reached 0.82 ROC-AUC and produced a ranked high-risk list for care-coordination prioritization.

twists.title: Integration was harder than modeling
twists.text: The same patient appeared across multiple tables and care episodes with conflicting timing.

twists.title: Leakage changed the evaluation
twists.text: Future information had to be removed before performance could be trusted.

twists.title: A score was not enough
twists.text: The final output emphasized ranked patients and understandable risk factors.

title: Medical Image Analyzer
subtitle: Designing two reliable explanations from one clinical image
problem: Clinicians and patients need different outputs from the same X-ray, while raw multimodal prompts can produce inconsistent structure and language.
approach: I treated prompt design like interface design: separate audiences, explicit roles, structured sections, and secure handling.
built: A clinical-report prompt, a plain-language explanation prompt, a Streamlit workflow, and secure API configuration.
value: One image produced both a structured professional report and a clearer patient-facing explanation.

twists.title: One answer could not serve two audiences
twists.text: Clinical precision and plain-language understanding required separate prompt paths.

twists.title: Structure improved reliability
twists.text: Explicit output sections reduced variation more than a generic request for a better answer.

twists.title: Prompting was product design
twists.text: The challenge was building a repeatable experience around model capability.

title: Behavioral Risk & Bed Demand
subtitle: Protecting population patterns while forecasting regional capacity
problem: 212,000+ records included more than 10,000 missing values. Naive imputation risked distorting population-level patterns.
approach: I designed cleaning around preserving distributions, then compared linear and nonlinear models for demand forecasting.
built: Structured imputation, Gradient Boosting, Ridge Regression, and Tableau dashboards.
value: Behavioral indicators were translated into interpretable regional demand and capacity-strain signals.

twists.title: Missing data was a modeling decision
twists.text: The imputation method could materially change the population story.

twists.title: Two model families improved judgment
twists.text: Ridge supported interpretation while Gradient Boosting captured nonlinear patterns.

twists.title: The dashboard completed the workflow
twists.text: Forecasts became useful only after they were translated into planning views.

title: Hospitality Revenue Dashboard
subtitle: Standardizing hotel performance before visualizing it
problem: More than 10 properties used disconnected spreadsheets and inconsistent KPI definitions, making cross-location comparisons unreliable.
approach: I began with stakeholder requirements and KPI definitions, then designed the analytical model before the dashboard.
built: A star-schema SQL model, standardized property data, Power BI dashboards, and DAX measures for RevPAR, DBRN, occupancy, and revenue.
value: Management gained self-service cross-property performance visibility from one consistent KPI layer.

twists.title: The KPI dictionary came first
twists.text: A polished dashboard would still be wrong if each property defined performance differently.

twists.title: The semantic layer created trust
twists.text: Standard definitions made cross-location comparison possible.

twists.title: Self-service changed the value
twists.text: The dashboard reduced dependence on disconnected manual reports.

title: HIV Epidemiological Database
subtitle: Creating a governed foundation for cross-country analysis
problem: CDC, World Bank, and UNAIDS published data in different formats, country conventions, indicator definitions, and time ranges.
approach: I treated source integration as a governance problem, resolving entities, indicators, lineage, and reproducibility.
built: Five integrated sources, six normalized MySQL/PostgreSQL tables, ER schemas, data dictionaries, and governance rules.
value: Researchers could perform reproducible longitudinal and cross-country analysis from one documented database.

twists.title: Country names were data-quality issues
twists.text: Small naming differences prevented reliable joins across global sources.

twists.title: Definitions mattered as much as values
twists.text: Indicators with similar names did not always measure the same thing.

twists.title: Documentation was part of the product
twists.text: Lineage and data dictionaries made the database reusable by others.

title: Ride-Share Demand Segmentation
subtitle: Finding behavior patterns inside 693,000+ ride records
problem: Ride prices varied widely, but there was no clear segmentation of user behavior or pricing drivers.
approach: I grouped rides by behavioral patterns first, then modeled pricing drivers within and across those segments.
built: K-Means clustering, three demand tiers, and Random Forest regression across time, distance, and pricing conditions.
value: The analysis revealed distinct demand behaviors and achieved RMSE 8.36 for pricing prediction.

twists.title: One average hid several behaviors
twists.text: Segmentation showed that one-size-fits-all pricing analysis was misleading.

twists.title: Clustering came before prediction
twists.text: The groups provided context for interpreting pricing drivers.

twists.title: Python only
twists.text: The project was completed in Python without adding tools that were not actually used.

title: Fashion-MNIST Classifier API
subtitle: Turning a computer-vision model into a deployable prediction service
problem: A high-performing image classifier is not useful to others when it only runs inside a notebook. The challenge was to make inference reliable, repeatable, and accessible through an API.
approach: I separated training from serving, validated the model on unseen images, and designed the deployment around a lightweight prediction endpoint.
built: A ResNet18 classifier trained on 60,000 Fashion-MNIST images, a FastAPI top-k inference endpoint, Gunicorn serving, Docker and Docker Compose packaging, and GCP deployment patterns.
value: The project moved from model experimentation to a reusable microservice that could be called by another application.

twists.title: Accuracy was only the first milestone
twists.text: The larger learning came from packaging the model so another system could call it consistently.

twists.title: Training and inference needed different workflows
twists.text: The notebook optimized learning, while the API needed fast loading, validation, and predictable output.

twists.title: Deployment exposed hidden assumptions
twists.text: File formats, preprocessing steps, label order, and model version all had to be preserved outside the training environment.

title: Amazon Review Sentiment Analyzer
subtitle: Converting thousands of product reviews into clear quality signals
problem: More than 17,000 customer reviews contained repeated product complaints, but manual reading could not reliably identify the categories and themes driving negative sentiment.
approach: I cleaned and tokenized the review text, trained a BERT-based classifier, and connected sentiment predictions to product-level interpretation.
built: A TensorFlow BERT pipeline, preprocessing and evaluation workflow, subcategory analysis, and a Gradio interface for interactive review classification.
value: The system reached 91% classification accuracy and surfaced durability complaints across two product subcategories as a concrete quality-improvement signal.

twists.title: A sentiment score was not the final insight
twists.text: The useful question was which product areas repeatedly generated negative experiences.

twists.title: Class performance mattered more than one headline metric
twists.text: I reviewed where the classifier confused neutral and negative language instead of relying only on overall accuracy.

twists.title: The interface changed the project
twists.text: Gradio turned the model from a notebook result into something a non-technical user could test directly.
